newsitem.title: USA: OPTIONS - US bond vols claw back above 9.0 percent.
newsitem.headline: OPTIONS - US bond vols claw back above 9.0 percent.

text.p: Implied volatilities for at-the-money options on U.S. Treasury bond futures climbed above 9.0 percent Wednesday for the first time in several weeks, but analysts were loath to declare an uptrend.
Rather, traders and analysts stressed bond vols were just returning to typical levels after several weeks of unusually low readings.
"Everybody has been talking about how cheap it is for so long that it has finally started to climb back to normal," said one options trader for a U.S. banking firm.
Key events for the interest rate markets next week are the employment cost index on Tuesday, gross domestic product report on Wednesday and employment data on Friday.
Analysts said they expected volatility to remain at tame levels, unlikely to break 8.0 percent on the downside or 10.0 percent on the upside.

One analyst for a U.S. brokerage house argued the recent sideways price action in the underlying futures represents a break in the downward price trend and therefore was boosting volatility after recent weak economic data reopened the debate over the likelihood of more Federal Reserve tightening moves.

Volatility levels have also been rising at the short end of the interest rate curve, particularly in short-dated midcurve options, which expire in 1997 but are priced from 1998 futures. June midcurve volatility jumped 1.0 point to 17.0 percent late in the session, and September was up 0.3 point at 16.6 percent.
For quarterly options, September volatility was steady at 10.7 percent while December climbed 0.4 point to 12.7 percent.

One trading firm was busy in both bond and Eurodollar options, buying 4,000 short-dated June 93.00 puts and selling 2,000 short-dated May 93.00 puts in Euros, and also buying June bond combo spreads and straddles in large size.
